# MCG 2-31-72: A Long Shadow in Virgo

*An edge-on galaxy offers a slender target for spring skies—and a reminder that a galaxy’s measured motion is not always a simple yardstick for its distance.*

In the spring sky, Virgo gathers galaxies like faint lights along a celestial road. Among them is **MCG 2-31-72**, also cataloged as NGC 4216: a broad, flattened island of stars seen nearly edge-on. Its light reaches us from a disk more than 11 arcminutes long but only about 2.3 arcminutes wide. In a telescope, that unequal measure hints at the view: not a round glow, but a thin streak set against the dark.

The galaxy’s catalog position is right ascension 12 hours 15 minutes 54.4 seconds, declination +13 degrees 08 minutes 58 seconds (J2000). Its listed visual magnitude is about 10. That number can be misleading at the eyepiece. The light is spread across an elongated shape, so MCG 2-31-72 may be harder to detect than a compact object of the same total brightness. Under a dark sky, look for a narrow haze rather than a sharply defined edge or a bright, obvious center.

There is a small puzzle in its motion. SIMBAD lists a heliocentric radial velocity of roughly 143 kilometers per second and a redshift of 0.000477. Redshift describes how much the galaxy’s light is shifted toward longer wavelengths; for distant galaxies, it often helps estimate distance. But at such a low velocity, a galaxy’s own motion relative to its surroundings can matter substantially. The number is a measurement of motion along our line of sight—not a straightforward cosmic speedometer.

SIMBAD classifies NGC 4216 as an active galaxy nucleus, or AGN. That label points to energetic activity in the galaxy’s central region, not to a promise that the center will stand out visually. Through an amateur telescope, the galaxy is a challenge of faint, diffuse light; its catalog classification belongs to a different kind of observation.

For a practical search, begin with Virgo on a clear spring evening. The coordinates are a more reliable guide than expecting the object to leap out from a star field: use a chart or mount capable of locating the position, then sweep slowly at low to moderate power. Once found, increase magnification only if the sky and telescope allow the faint shape to hold steady. Averted vision—looking slightly to one side of the target—may help reveal the disk. Give your eyes time to adjust, and shield them from nearby lights. If the galaxy remains elusive, try again when it is higher above the horizon or under darker skies.

The reward may be subtle: a slim smudge, almost easy to mistake for a flaw in the view. Yet that fragile line of light is a whole galaxy, its starlight gathered across an immense disk and carried to a small patch of sky. A careful observer does not need to see its central activity or resolve individual stars. Finding the shape is enough.

**Source:** SIMBAD entry for NGC 4216: https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=NGC%204216
